issues.legal_issue: An arbitration agreement, award, and decree concerning a minor’s inherited property are void when the minor is represented by a relative who is neither a lawful guardian nor a court-appointed guardian and the minor’s interests are not protected.
material_facts: A minor heir was represented in the arbitration and the proceedings to confirm its award by his adult brother.
The brother was not a lawful guardian under Mohammedan law and there was no order appointing him as guardian.
The brother relinquished the minor’s rights in property without legal authority, and the minor’s interests were not protected despite a conflict of interest.
issues.conclusion: The arbitration agreement, award, and decree confirming the award were void and did not bind the minor.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mohammedan law, a brother is not a lawful guardian of a minor’s property; in default of a legal guardian, a court may appoint one to protect the minor’s property. A relative’s unauthorized compromise is not binding on the minor. The Court relied on Mohd. Amin v. Vakil Ahmed and Imambandi v. Mutsaddi.

rule.if: inheritance_partition_proceeding and minor_heir_involved and minor_represented_by_unauthorized_relative and minor_interests_unprotected

predicates.inheritance_partition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the division of an inherited estate among heirs.
predicates.minor_heir_involved: An heir whose property interests are at issue is a minor.
predicates.minor_represented_by_unauthorized_relati: A relative who is neither a lawful guardian nor appointed by a court acts for the minor.
predicates.minor_interests_unprotected: The minor’s interests are not legally protected in the proceeding or compromise.

issues.definition: When an inheritance-division proceeding affects a minor represented by an unauthorized relative and the minor’s interests are unprotected, the arbitration agreement, award, and confirming decree are void as to the minor.

issues.legal_issue: A co-owner’s limitation period for seeking recovery of an inherited share does not run from the deceased owner’s death but from an express ouster or denial of title.
material_facts: The heirs succeeded to the deceased owner’s estate as co-owners in specific shares.
The heirs continued to hold the estate without dividing it.
The evidence did not establish that the claimant knew of an express denial of title or had been openly excluded from the properties.
issues.conclusion: The claimant’s partition claim was not barred merely because time had passed since the deceased owner’s death or because another co-owner possessed the properties.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 144 of Schedule I to the Limitation Act, 1908, limitation for a co-owner’s claim to recover a share runs from express ouster or denial of title, not from the deceased owner’s death. Co-heirs take as tenants in common in specific shares. The Court also referred to Monsharam Chakravarty v. Gonesh Chandra Chakravarty concerning the recurring cause of action for partition.

rule.if: co_owner_partition_proceeding and heirs_hold_property_in_common and not open_ouster_or_denial_of_title

predicates.co_owner_partition_proceeding: The proceeding seeks division or recovery of a share in property held by co-owners.
predicates.heirs_hold_property_in_common: The heirs succeeded to the estate as co-owners and continued to hold it without division.
predicates.open_ouster_or_denial_of_title: A co-owner openly and unequivocally denies the claimant’s title or excludes the claimant from the property.

issues.definition: A co-owner’s share claim is not time-barred by the deceased owner’s death or another co-owner’s possession alone when the heirs continue to hold the property in common and there has been no open ouster or denial of title.

issues.legal_issue: Fraudulent concealment of a claimant’s right to sue postpones the start of limitation until the claimant discovers the concealed right or title.
material_facts: One heir knew that properties treated during the partition proceedings as religious endowment property were in fact part of the deceased owner’s inheritable estate.

That heir represented the properties as endowment property, obtained a partition award and decree on that basis, and concealed a later official determination that the properties were not endowment property.
The claimant did not know, and could not with reasonable diligence have discovered, the properties’ true character until learning of the concealment.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could rely on section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1908; limitation was computed from discovery of the fraud, and the claim was not barred.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1908 provides that where fraud keeps a person from knowledge of a right to sue or the title on which it is founded, limitation is computed from discovery of the fraud. The Court relied on the principle in Rolfe v. Gregory, as restated in Boman Chandra Datta v. Promotha Nath Ghose, and on Rahimboy v. Turner concerning the defendant’s burden to show the claimant’s clear and definite knowledge of the fraud. It also referred to Halsbury’s Laws of England on fraud as a ground for setting aside a judgment.

predicates.fraud_limitation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a claim is barred by limitation where fraud is alleged.
predicates.defendant_active_concealment_of_claimant: The defendant knowingly conceals or misrepresents facts that keep the claimant from knowing a right to sue or the title supporting it.
predicates.claimant_unaware_of_right_despite_reason: The claimant does not know of the right or title and could not have discovered it through reasonable diligence before the fraud became known.

issues.definition: When a defendant’s active concealment keeps a claimant who exercised reasonable diligence unaware of a right to sue, limitation is computed from the claimant’s discovery of the fraud.

issues.legal_issue: Possession by one co-owner is not adverse to another co-owner without an unequivocal, open denial of the other’s title and exclusion of that co-owner.
material_facts: The other co-owners had been kept from knowing the properties’ true character, and the evidence did not show that they knew of an ouster.
There was no evidence that the possessor openly denied the other co-owners’ title or excluded them from the properties.
issues.conclusion: The plea of adverse possession failed.
issues.legal_principle: Possession by one co-owner is presumed to be possession for all co-owners unless it is shown to be hostile to them through denial of their title and exclusion of them. Ouster requires an unequivocal act asserting title and an open denial of the entitled parties’ rights.

rule.if: co_owner_adverse_possession_proceeding and one_co_owner_possesses_property and not open_unequivocal_ouster

predicates.co_owner_adverse_possession_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim that one co-owner acquired the property against another by adverse possession.
predicates.one_co_owner_possesses_property: A co-owner possesses property also claimed by other co-owners.
predicates.open_unequivocal_ouster: The possessor openly and unequivocally denies the other co-owners’ title and excludes them from the property.

issues.definition: A co-owner’s possession does not establish adverse possession against other co-owners unless it includes an open and unequivocal ouster of them.

issues.legal_issue: A prior partition award and decree cannot prevent reopening partition when they treated inheritable property as non-partitionable endowment property through fraud and later-discovered facts establish its true character.
material_facts: The heirs consented to an award and decree treating certain properties as religious endowment property that was not partible.
The properties were later established to be part of the deceased owner’s inheritable estate rather than endowment property.
The misclassification resulted from one heir’s knowing misrepresentation and concealment, and the other heirs learned the true character of the properties later.
issues.conclusion: The declaration in the award and decree that the properties were endowment property could not stand; the entire partition had to be reopened, and the decree was no obstacle to the partition claim.
issues.legal_principle: A judgment may be set aside for fraud where facts discovered after judgment make success of the action reasonably probable; the Court relied on Birch v. Birch. Under Mohammedan law, heirs inherit definite fractions of every part of the estate as tenants in common, and the doctrine of partial partition does not apply. The cause of action for partition is perpetually recurring, as discussed in Monsharam Chakravarty v. Gonesh Chandra Chakravarty.

predicates.inherited_property_partition_proceeding: The proceeding seeks partition of property claimed as part of a deceased person’s estate.
predicates.prior_partition_based_on_fraudulent_misc: A prior award or decree treated the property as non-partitionable based on a knowing misrepresentation or concealment of its character.
predicates.later_discovered_facts_establish_inherit: Facts discovered after the prior decision establish that the property was part of the deceased person’s inheritable estate.

issues.definition: When a prior partition decision rests on a fraudulent misclassification and later-discovered facts establish that the property was inheritable, that decision does not bar reopening partition.
